chapter: Arranging, Fletcher Henderson and Lucky Millinder
title: Henderson's lessons in basic fundamentals; turning down staff arranging
summary: Henderson showed him simple voicing in exchange for copying; Thompson declined a Basie arranging job demanding three arrangements a week because he wanted to be a player.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But any way, that was Fletcher Henderson's nickname, Smack.
As you said. Yes, well he was also -- as I've told you, a lot of these great musicians -- you'd be surprised, if they liked you they would tell you things, which

was like getting free information that would cost you a million dollars or you would have to go to school for for years to learn. And like I said, in a very short time Fletcher Henderson straightened me out on how to voice music which I had been trying to use my original ideas and things I'd heard other guys do which seemed to make a band sound bigger, you know. But it was a more complicated way of doing it. Fletcher Henderson showed me the simple way of doing it, which was very simple. Just basic fundamentals of music, just like any athletic sports.

Like you hear the basketball players in particular talk about -- or golfers. They always talk about coming back to the basic principles and fundamentals of the sport, you know. If it's basketball they come back to the basic fundamentals of their game, like the Boston Celtics, if we may go into this a little deeper, they have their fast running breaks and they work a team to death fast, and they pass and they're tricky and they can shoot well, you know. They put all that together when they find themselves frustrated. The same way with a golfer. When he finds himself hitting a ball in the woods instead of trying to hit it long and far, he comes back to try and hit it straight and in the middle, and putting feeling in his wrist, and chipping at the ball so he can one-putt, you know, things of that sort. That's what I mean by the basic fundamentals.

Yes, as I said, Fletcher Henderson taught me those basic fundamentals, and he did it as an extra bonus payment for me for copying his music that he needed very badly and quickly. Because he was writing for Benny Goodman when he was playing in the Coconut Grove, Ambassador Hotel, and you know, many times they'd have to change the copyist arrangement around and he needed a quick copies, like, you know, that was able to do this. And you know, as payment to me and you know, as a friendly gesture he showed me what he could show me, which was really appreciated by me. And as I said, through this knowledge that I learned then I was able to write these arrangements later for bands like Count Basie, and which was flattering to me. And -- but I didn't want to travel under those circumstances, because I didn't think I could do justice in writing, being required to write as many as three arrangements a week for a basic salary, of a minimum salary. And so rather than to do a sloppy job, as I saw some of the fellas doing and trying to keep up with this requirement, I decided against it. And in fact I'm sort of happy that I did because I don't think -- I might have missed getting the experience of playing with these great musicians like Lester Young and Coleman Hawkins had I kept into that field of just writing. And I wanted to be a player.
But I hadn't really still gotten enough experience as a player, you know.
